title.rendered: Dependabot version updates support Agent Package Manager

content.rendered:
You can now keep your AI agent skills, prompts, and instructions up to date with Dependabot version updates for Agent Package Manager (APM).

Dependabot opens pull requests to update supported git dependencies declared in apm.yml and regenerates apm.lock.yaml when it’s present. This support covers version updates, not security updates.

Get started

Add an apm entry to your .github/dependabot.yml file, specify the directory containing apm.yml, and choose an update schedule.

APM support is generally available on github.com for all GitHub plans and will be available in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more

  • Configuring Dependabot version updates
  • Supported APM dependencies and update behavior
  • Community discussion on APM support

title.rendered: GitHub Actions adds multi-cloud compute to improve reliability

content.rendered:
We’re expanding the infrastructure behind GitHub-hosted runners so your workflows start faster and run more reliably, even during periods of peak demand. GitHub Actions now schedules eligible jobs across a broader, multi-cloud compute pool. This adds capacity, reduces capacity-related queue times, and improves service resilience. As part of this, eligible Linux jobs may run on Amazon Web Services (AWS) in addition to Microsoft Azure.

Multi-cloud compute will be used for standard 2-core and 4-core Linux runners and compatible 2-core and 4-core larger runners without specialized configurations. This change does not apply to Windows runners or runners with private networking or other specialized configurations.

For customers on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, and GitHub Team, eligible runners will automatically use multi-cloud compute. Customers on GitHub Enterprise Cloud can opt in by going to Enterprise Settings > Policies > Actions > General > Hosted compute cloud providers and enabling AWS compute.

Editor’s note (November 2, 2026): Corrected the path for opting in.

GitHub Actions automatically schedules eligible jobs across available cloud providers. Your existing runner labels and workflow syntax remain unchanged.

Recommended action: Keep your network allowlists up to date

To get the full benefit of expanded capacity, make sure any IP allowlists or network-based access policies your workflows rely on include all published GitHub Actions IP ranges. Runners in the expanded compute pool use additional outbound IP addresses, so policies that allow only Azure or Microsoft-owned ranges, including Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, can block connections or authentication from these runners.

This is a rolling change, so we recommend updating your allowlists now, before your workflows begin running in the expanded compute pool.

All GitHub Actions runner IP ranges, including the new ones, are published in the actions array returned by GET https://api.github.com/meta. We recommend keeping your allowlists in sync with this endpoint rather than relying on cloud-provider-specific ranges. See GitHub-hosted runner IP addresses for details.

title.rendered: pull_request_target blocked by default December 2

content.rendered:
Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026.

GitHub introduced this default rule through workflow execution protections. The rule initially runs in evaluate mode, so you can see which workflow runs it would block before enforcement begins.

Private and internal repositories aren’t affected.

Why we’re making this change

pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can access its secrets. If a workflow executes untrusted code from a fork, that code could compromise your pipeline or steal secrets. The default rule helps reduce this risk while letting you explicitly allow workflows that depend on the trigger.

Brownout schedule

Before permanent enforcement begins on December 2, 2026, we’ll temporarily enforce the default protection during two scheduled brownouts. These windows will help you identify affected workflows and update your policies before enforcement becomes permanent.

Date Time (UTC)
November 9, 2026 16:00–18:00
November 16, 2026 16:00–18:00

During each window, pull_request_target workflow attempts blocked by the default rule in affected public repositories will create failed runs with an error annotation; the workflows won’t execute. After each window, the default rule will return to evaluate mode, allowing workflows to run with warnings. Private and internal repositories aren’t affected.

Prepare your workflows

Before the first brownout on November 9, use Insights to see which workflow runs the rule would block. From there, you have two options:

  • Keep the default rule in place to block pull_request_target.
  • Explicitly allow pull_request_target in an applicable Actions event policy if your workflows depend on it. Use workflow file targeting to allow specific workflows.

See how to control workflow execution to configure your policies.

This change applies to public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, not GitHub Enterprise Server.

title.rendered: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles are generally available

content.rendered:
You can now use GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles in general availability on GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Lockfiles let you keep readable tag and branch references in your workflows while running the exact commits you locked, even if those references move.

This release brings the capabilities introduced in the public preview to general availability:

  • Lock your dependencies: Use the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to generate .github/workflows/actions.lock for actions and their transitive dependencies.
  • Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and runs its recorded commit.
  • Keep updates in sync: When Dependabot opens a version update for an action in an onboarded workflow, it also regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, without additional configuration.
  • Require lockfile: Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can use the Require lockfile policy to enforce adoption.
  • Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that your lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check.

Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes, but they don’t determine whether a dependency is safe. Review dependencies before locking them.

Get started

Install the extension from the gh-actions-lock repository, then review and commit the generated lockfile and workflow changes. See workflow dependency lockfiles in GitHub Docs for details and setup instructions.

Share feedback in the community discussion or report an issue with the extension.

title.rendered: GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles in public preview

content.rendered:
GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, Team, and Free plans. Tags and branches can move after you review a workflow, so a later run might execute different code. Lockfiles let you keep those references in your workflow while running the exact commits you locked.

Editor’s note (October 14th, 2026): Updated which plans have access to this public preview.

If an action is compromised, a moved tag or branch can introduce malicious code into your workflow without a change to your repository. Lockfiles help protect against unexpected dependency changes by keeping workflow runs tied to the commits you locked. Locking does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe, so review dependencies before locking them.

Install the gh actions-lock extension for the GitHub CLI to create and maintain your workflow lockfile. With the extension, you can:

  • Pin your dependencies: Generate .github/workflows/actions.lock with reviewable commits for actions and their transitive dependencies.
  • Adopt locking gradually: Onboard workflows individually. Once onboarded, a workflow must have lockfile entries for its dependencies, and GitHub Actions runs the recorded commits.
  • Keep workflow runs consistent: GitHub Actions requires each dependency of an onboarded workflow to be in the lockfile and uses its recorded commit, even if a tag or branch moves.
  • Check for stale lockfiles: Verify that the lockfile is up to date without modifying files, including in a CI check.

The Require lockfile policy is also available in public preview. Enterprise, organization, and repository administrators can require workflows to use lockfiles across their enterprise, organization, or repository.

Keep locked dependencies up to date with Dependabot

Dependabot helps you keep your GitHub Actions dependencies up to date. When it opens a version update for an action in a workflow that is already onboarded, it also regenerates the matching lockfile entry in the same pull request, keeping the updated workflow reference and its locked commit in sync without additional configuration. Read more about Dependabot updates for actions.

Get started

To get started, install the extension from the public gh-actions-lock repository, then review and commit the generated lockfile and workflow changes.

For more details and links to setup instructions, see workflow dependency lockfiles in GitHub Docs.

Share feedback in the existing community discussion or open an issue in the gh-actions-lock repository.

Thank you to the community members who helped shape this preview through testing and feedback, with special thanks to Andrew Nesbitt, François Proulx, Jesse Houwing, and William Woodruff for their close collaboration and iteration on this solution over the past year.

title.rendered: Prioritize Dependabot alerts with reachability analysis

content.rendered:
Dependabot alerts can add up faster than a team can work through them. A vulnerable package in your dependency tree doesn’t always mean your code uses the vulnerable part of it, so knowing whether it does gives you more context when deciding where to start.

Reachability analysis for Dependabot, now in public preview for JavaScript and TypeScript, adds that context to your alerts. It looks for call paths from your code to the vulnerable functions in your dependencies and shows the evidence on each alert. Use it alongside severity, EPSS score, production context, and your own knowledge of your application to prioritize and remediate dependency vulnerabilities in the way that works for your team.

How it works

Dependabot runs reachability analysis for you in a managed GitHub Actions workflow, so there’s nothing to install or maintain. For each advisory, the analysis uses curated data that identifies the vulnerable functions in the affected package. CodeQL builds a call graph across your repository and its dependencies, then searches it for a path from your code to each of those functions.

Each open Dependabot alert gets one of these verdicts:

  • Reachable: Your code has at least one call path to the vulnerable function.
  • Potentially reachable: The analysis couldn’t determine whether your code calls the vulnerable function. Treat these alerts as reachable.
  • Unreachable: The analysis completed and found no call path to the vulnerable function. These alerts are lower priority.
  • Reachability unavailable: The alert couldn’t be analyzed. Triage it as you normally would.

Verdicts appear on the Dependabot alerts you already use, and they never close or dismiss an alert. Filter and sort by verdict on the repository and organization alerts pages, or use the Dependabot alerts REST API to bring the same signal into your own tools and agents.

Availability and requirements

During the public preview:

  • Cost: Free. You don’t need a GitHub Advanced Security license and you aren’t billed for the GitHub Actions minutes the analysis uses.
  • Plans: GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.
  • Languages: JavaScript and TypeScript with an npm, Yarn, or pnpm lockfile in the repository.
  • Runners: The analysis runs on GitHub-hosted runners. Self-hosted runners aren’t supported during the preview. As with Dependabot updates, you don’t need to turn on GitHub Actions for the analysis to run.
  • Repository size and code complexity: Some monorepos and/or repositories with manifest files in multiple directories may not be supported during the preview. During the preview, if analysis runs for longer than three hours, some results might show “Reachability unavailable”.
  • Advisory coverage: All GitHub-reviewed JavaScript advisories from the GitHub Advisory Database that receive Dependabot alerts are covered.

Get started

Reachability analysis is off by default. Turn it on for many repositories at once with a custom security configuration for your enterprise or organization, or for a single repository in the Dependabot section of Settings > Advanced Security. Dependabot alerts must be on to see reachability verdicts.

The first scan starts right away and can take from a few minutes to a few hours. Scans then rerun daily while the repository has open Dependabot alerts, so verdicts keep up as your code and advisories change.

To learn more, see About reachability analysis for Dependabot alerts in GitHub Docs.

If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment in our Community discussion.

title.rendered: GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available

content.rendered:
GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions.

Define your automation in natural language Markdown files, and GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles them into standard Actions YAML. Because these are GitHub Actions, they reuse your existing runner groups and policy constraints. You can use GitHub Copilot or bring your own coding agent to power each workflow.

We’ve been rolling out our agentic developer workflows, and the results are measurable. One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone. Across his team, measured velocity has more than doubled on average, and AI now authors 91% of the team’s commits. With these workflows, the team cut production errors from about 11,000 a day to under 1,000 and drove a technology migration end to end.

One workflow takes a feature from requirements to implementation with validation evidence. Others keep our frameworks current and steadily raise code quality and test coverage. Because AI drives the process to completion, our engineers can run four or five efforts in parallel and stay focused on the bigger goals.
Ben Alton – Senior manager, Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team at Accenture

Built-in safeguards

GitHub Agentic Workflows incorporates layered safeguards for your automation. Agents access GitHub content respecting the integrity filter rules, run with read-only permissions by default, and execute inside a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall. The outputs are validated through the safe outputs process, and a dedicated threat detection job scans all proposed changes before they are applied.

Additional capabilities for general availability

Highlights since the public preview include:

  • Actions Runner Controller (ARC) and Docker-in-Docker support: Run agentic workflows on self-hosted ARC runners with Docker-in-Docker.
  • Improved budget forecasting: gh aw forecast is no longer experimental. It now includes both threat detection credits and monthly ranges for a fuller picture of your AI credit spend.
  • New models, engine choices, and workflows: The model inventory has been refreshed, model providers can be picked per workflow, and there are new workflow templates that can be added with gh aw add-wizard.
  • Model routing: Workflows can use a model router that optimizes for task type and difficulty.
  • Improved agent isolation: Agents can run in a Cloud Hypervisor or NVX micro-VM and prevent data leaks in cross-repository workflows with enclaves.

See the GitHub Agentic Workflows release notes for the full list of changes.

Get started

Follow the quickstart guide to install the CLI extension and trigger your first workflow in minutes. Explore prebuilt workflows in GitHub Next’s agentics repository for ready-to-use examples covering triage, dependency management, code review, and reporting.

GitHub Agentic Workflows is now generally available on github.com for GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise. Using the default GitHub Copilot CLI engine to power a workflow requires a Copilot license.

Learn more in the GitHub Agentic Workflows documentation, and join the conversation in the community discussion.

title.rendered: GitHub package firewall in public preview

content.rendered:
Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): Rewrote the changelog for clarity and added imagery.

There’s been a recent flood of malware attacks that exploit systems at package installation time. Agents and CI runners are particularly vulnerable to these attacks because they install dependencies to accomplish a task or complete a build without a human in the loop. To stem this tide, GitHub is introducing a new package firewall, which sits between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories. The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate. The package firewall is available today in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

How it works

First, administrators set policy controls for their enterprise. The controls available today include a configurable cooldown period, checking the GitHub Advisory Database for malware or vulnerability advisories, and supply-chain checks like attestation downgrades.

Then, endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of pointing directly at the upstream package registries. Metadata requests for package lists as well as the actual package downloads flow through the firewall, which evaluates them against the policy. If a package is blocked erroneously, the user can request an exception with a workflow similar to other GitHub Advanced Security features.

Availability and limitations

The package firewall is available in public preview as we scale up the infrastructure behind it and continue to add features based on customer demand. It is available to GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. The service is free while in the preview period. When it reaches general availability, it will be charged based on metered usage, similar to Actions billing.

Currently the package firewall only supports npm packages.

How to use it

For detailed setup instructions, see Protecting endpoints with package firewall. Join the discussion in GitHub Community.

title.rendered: Workflow execution protections in GitHub Actions generally available

content.rendered:
Workflow execution protections for GitHub Actions, previously in public preview, are now generally available for GitHub Enterprise, organizations, and repositories.

Execution protections let you define an allowlist that controls who can trigger an Actions workflow and what events can start it. Actor rules cover the who, event rules cover the what, and actions evaluate both before a run.

What’s new

Alongside the actor and event rules you’ve used in public preview, general availability adds:

  • Workflow file targeting: Scope execution protection rules to specific workflow files rather than an entire repository, so a single repository can apply different policies to different workflows. For example, restrict deploy.yml to a designated team while leaving CI workflows open to all contributors.
  • Insights: See how actions evaluate and enforce your rules across your enterprise, organization, and repositories. This enables you to audit policy impact and tune rules both before and after you enforce them.
  • REST API: Manage execution protections programmatically at the enterprise, organization, and repository level. Create, read, update, and delete rules — including workflow path conditions — so you can manage Actions policy as code, keep rules consistent across hundreds of repositories, and wire enforcement into your existing governance tooling instead of clicking through settings.

Evaluate mode also carries over from the preview, so you can run rules in shadow mode and see which workflow runs would be blocked before you enforce them.

New secure defaults

Vulnerabilities in pull_request_target workflows, such as Pwn Requests, are one of the most commonly exploited vulnerabilities in action workflows. pull_request_target runs with access to your secrets in the context of the base repository, so if code is executed from a fork, that untrusted code could poison your pipeline and exfiltrate secrets. We’re rolling out a default protection rule to limit the execution of pull_request_target events.

For public repositories that do not already have an applicable event policy, GitHub is introducing a default rule that disables pull_request_target. This default does not apply to private or internal repositories. It initially runs in evaluate mode, so you can see which workflow runs would be affected before enforcement begins.

On December 2nd, 2026, we’ll automatically enforce the default rule for affected repositories that were using the default pull_request_target policy before general availability.

Editor’s note (October 21, 2026): We updated the automatic enforcement date for the default pull_request_target rule to December 2nd, 2026.

To prepare for the roll out of this rule, you can view the results of the evaluate rule using Insights and see which workflow runs will fail once enforcement begins.

From there you have two options: leave the rule in place to block pull_request_target, or explicitly allow pull_request_target in an applicable Actions event policy if your workflows still depend on the trigger. Specific workflows can be allow-listed using the new workflow file targeting.

To get started, see About Actions policies, Control workflow execution, and the Actions policies REST API reference.

title.rendered: Bulk migrate branch protections to rulesets for a repository

content.rendered:
You can now convert all branch protection rules of a repository to rulesets in a single action. This is an extension of the ability to convert a single branch protection rule to a ruleset that we released previously, now allowing for at-scale conversions.

How it works

Navigate to Settings → Rulesets in your repository and click Import branch protection rules. In the Review import dialog, you can:

  • Preview the rulesets that will be created before you confirm the conversion.
  • See which branch protection rules are already covered by an existing ruleset.
  • Review cases where one branch protection rule produces multiple rulesets to preserve its original behavior.
  • Choose an enforcement status (e.g., Active, Evaluate, or Disabled) and select which rulesets to create.

After you click Create rulesets, choose whether to keep or delete the original branch protection rules.

Why migrate to rulesets?

Rulesets offer several advantages over classic branch protections:

  • Apply rules across multiple branches with pattern matching
  • Layer multiple rulesets for granular policy control
  • Manage rulesets at the organization or enterprise level
  • Configure fine-grained bypass permissions for users, teams, and apps

Availability

This feature is available for all repositories where rulesets are available. Learn more about converting your branch protections to repository rulesets.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

title.rendered: Dependabot alerts REST API now includes dependency versions

content.rendered:
You can now get the version of a vulnerable dependency directly from Dependabot alert responses in the REST API. Each alert’s dependency object includes a new version_requirement field with the version or version constraint that Dependabot last recorded for the alert.

Alert responses already included the advisory’s vulnerable version range, but not the version in your repository. If you sync alerts to other security tools, you no longer need to parse lockfiles or make a separate GraphQL request for vulnerableRequirements to get that version.

The value depends on how Dependabot detected the dependency:

  • Lockfiles: The resolved version.
  • Manifests without a lockfile: The version or version constraint declared in the manifest.
  • Dependency submission API: The resolved version submitted by your build tooling.

The field is null when no value is available. If an alert covers more than one vulnerable version of a dependency, the field holds one recorded value and may not represent all of them. Long version constraints may also be truncated.

You’ll find version_requirement in responses for individual alerts, in repository, organization, and enterprise alert lists, and in dependabot_alert webhook payloads.

This field is available now on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts and the dependabot_alert webhook event.

title.rendered: Open source license compliance generally available

content.rendered:
Enterprises can now manage their dependencies’ licenses at scale with sophisticated, ruleset-based checks that enforce a centralized policy. Open source license compliance is now generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GHEC, for repositories with GitHub Code Security enabled.

How it works

Open source license compliance expands on the capabilities of the dependency review action by introducing an enterprise-wide license policy. The policy is activated by targeting repositories with a ruleset that uses a new Require license compliance results before merging condition, similar to the existing code scanning conditions. When developers open pull requests that add or modify dependencies, license checks automatically ensure each new or changed dependency has an acceptable license. The feature annotates the pull request with a message about each noncompliant dependencies. These annotations must be addressed by removing or replacing the dependency, amending the license policy, or creating package exceptions.

Open source license compliance introduces a new predefined enterprise role, Enterprise Open-Source License Manager. Assign this role to individuals or teams who should review and approve closure requests. Policy managers receive email notifications about pending requests and can review them from the enterprise console.

What’s new and improved

Since the public preview release in June, we’ve made several improvements:

  • License information is now available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud data residency customers. This not only enables the license compliance feature, but also populates the dependency graph and Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) exports with license data.
  • License policy changes now emit audit log events, for integration with external systems of record.
  • There are new API endpoints for downloading, updating, and replacing the enterprise license policy.
  • There is also a new API endpoint for checking whether packages comply with policy. This enables coding agents to avoid recommending or incorporating packages which violate an organization’s license usage policy.

How to try it

For detailed setup instructions, see About open source license compliance.

For information about API endpoints see REST API endpoints for dependency-graph

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

title.rendered: Xcode 27 runner image generally available

content.rendered:
You can now use the generally available Xcode 27 runner image to build and test your Apple applications in GitHub Actions. Previously in public preview, this GitHub-hosted image runs on macOS 27 and includes the Xcode 27 toolchain and Apple SDKs.

Xcode-based images

Each image supports one major Xcode version rather than targeting a specific operating system version. This makes it easier to select the toolchain your project needs and know what each runner provides.

Get started

To use the image, set your workflow’s runs-on: value to one of these labels:

  • xcode-27
  • xcode-27-xlarge

If you already use these labels, you don’t need to change your workflows. The image is available on Apple Silicon (arm64) runners only, not Intel runners.

To view the installed software or report an issue, visit the runner-images repository.

title.rendered: Confidential comments on repository security advisories

content.rendered:
You can now post confidential comments on repository security advisories. Confidential comments are visible only to people with write access to the repository, so you can discuss a report with your team without the reporter or other invited collaborators seeing it.

Previously, every comment on an advisory was visible to all of its collaborators, including the reporter. To discuss suspected abuse, investigation details, or coordination notes, you had to move the conversation somewhere else and lose it from the advisory’s history.

With this update:

  • Select Confidential. Only maintainers will see this comment below the comment box before you post.
  • Confidential comments are clearly marked in the advisory timeline.
  • Reporters and invited collaborators without write access can’t see confidential comments and aren’t notified about them.
  • Access follows current repository permissions. If someone loses write access, they can no longer read confidential comments.
  • Views of confidential comments are recorded in the audit log.

You can’t switch a comment between confidential and regular after you post it. Confidential comments are not currently available through the public GraphQL or REST APIs.

This is available for public repositories with private vulnerability reporting enabled on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

Learn more about repository security advisories.

title.rendered: GitHub App improvements for least privilege and management

content.rendered:
We’re releasing several GitHub Apps improvements today that help developers move off of classic PATs, improve GitHub App management, and request fewer sensitive permissions. We’ve also made it easier for repository administrators to use apps that their administrators have approved and updated the GitHub App credential management UI in advance of our planned workload federation features.

New repository creation and installation management permissions

Two new repository fine-grained permissions have been added, available to both fine-grained PATs and GitHub Apps.

  • repository_creation:write: Allows the caller to create a repository in the account where it’s granted.
  • installation_repositories: write: Allows the caller to add or remove that repository from an installation in the organization.

Create a repository without repository_administration

You can now use the repository_creation:write permission to create repositories without needing the broader repository_administration:write permission.

Previously, an app or PAT needed repository_administration:write to create a repository. That permission also grants other repository administration features like deletion and transfer. This could lead to administrators rejecting apps, banning PATs with this permission, or having to accept the over-privilege risk.

The new permission supports a least-privilege approach by granting only the ability to create repositories. When the repository is created, the app or user that created it will be given access to it. An app using this permission still requires an organization administrator to install the app.

See the API docs for repository creation in organizations, from a template, for the current user, with a fork, and via GraphQL.

Manage installation repositories with an app or fine-grained PAT

The Add a repository to an installation organization-level API and its corresponding removal API now support GitHub Apps and fine-grained PATs. Previously, these APIs only supported the coarse-grained repo scope.

These APIs support a new repository-level fine-grained permission:installation_repositories:write. Having this permission on a repository allows the caller to add or remove that repository from any installation in the organization. If the caller is a user, they must also be an organization owner or an administrator on the repository in question.

This allows organizations to build automation that controls which repositories are accessible to which GitHub Apps without relying on an administrator’s PAT with broad permissions.

Repository administrators can more easily add approved GitHub Apps to repositories

Historically, all apps that requested organization-level access were blocked from being installed on a repository by a repository administrator, no matter what. This restriction has been relaxed in the case where the app is already installed in the organization, meaning it’s been approved by an organization owner for that organization-level access. Repository administrators can now edit an existing installation to add their repositories to an app without requiring organization owner approval. The apps already have the organization-level access, so adding them to another repository in the organization doesn’t increase that access or give the repository administrator additional privileges.

With the addition of the repository_creation permission above, there are now three sensitive permission sets that require organization owner approval:

  • All organization-level permissions
  • Repository administration
  • Repository creation

This change allows repository administrators to better use apps that are already approved for use in their organization.

If you’d like to prevent repository administrators from adding apps to their repositories, see “Restricting GitHub App Installation to Organization Owners” in the docs. For more details on adding an app to a repository, see “Installing a GitHub App“.

Use offline_access with GitHub Apps to gradually reenable short-lived, rotating tokens

GitHub Apps now support the offline_access scope, like OAuth apps. While GitHub Apps use short-lived, rotating tokens by default, some developers have disabled expiration for convenience and now struggle to reenable it.

This support helps app developers gradually migrate to expiring user access tokens. Developers can enable token expiration for testing and rollout without having to switch every user to expiring tokens at the same time, which would break existing clients.

When offline_access is requested, the app receives a refresh token in addition to the expiring access token. It only changes that specific authentication and doesn’t impact future sessions.

The scope parameter is still otherwise unused for GitHub Apps—permissions are still statically selected on the application registration. For more details, see “Refreshing user access tokens“.

This is available in GHES 3.23.

GitHub Apps can fetch details about other private and internal apps

GitHub Apps can now use the Get an app API to fetch details about private and internal GitHub Apps, as long as they share some ownership.

The permitted access patterns are:

  1. Public apps: Any other app can fetch the app’s details. This was the previously enabled level of access.
  2. Apps in the same organization: Apps can fetch each other’s details regardless of visibility, if they share the same owner.
  3. Internal apps in the same enterprise: An internal app’s details can be fetched by another app in the same enterprise, even across organization boundaries.
  4. Enterprise-to-organization access: An enterprise-owned app can fetch details about apps owned by organizations in the same enterprise.

This enables organizations and enterprises to automate more of their GitHub App auditing and administration.

For more details about app visibility, see “Making a GitHub App public or private“.

A new credential management tab for GitHub Apps

GitHub App credentials are now managed from a dedicated Credentials tab instead of appearing inline with the rest of the app configuration. This makes credentials easier to find and manage, and sets aside space for our upcoming workload federation credentials.

These improvements will be available in GHES 3.24, with the exception of offline_access support, which will be included in GHES 3.23.

Let us know what you think in the GitHub Community.

title.rendered: Audit GitHub Code Quality finding dismissals and reopenings

content.rendered:
You can now review manual dismissals and reopenings of GitHub Code Quality findings in your organization or enterprise audit log. Findings may appear in either your repository’s default-branch backlog or pull requests. Two new events record these actions:

  • repo.code_quality_findings_dismissed records a dismissal of one or more backlog findings.
  • repo.code_quality_findings_reopened records a reopening of one or more backlog findings.

Each event includes who made the request, when it happened, the repository and rule, and the identifiers and count of the affected findings.

For repositories with Code Quality enabled, you don’t need additional setup. If you have access to your organization audit log or enterprise audit log, filter by these action names to review activity. On GitHub Enterprise Cloud, you can also retrieve these events through the audit log API.

This improvement is generally available on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including enterprises with data residency. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server. For more on managing findings, see Fixing code quality findings in your repository backlog.

Join the GitHub Community discussion.

title.rendered: Anonymous organization-level registries for Dependabot

content.rendered:
You can now select Anonymous as the authentication method for an organization-level private registry. Use it for registries that Dependabot can reach without credentials, such as an internal package mirror that allows anonymous reads.

On github.com, Dependabot update jobs can only reach hosts on the egress allowlist and the private registries you configure. A private registry that’s only defined in a file such as .npmrc or nuget.config is blocked. Organization-level registries apply to every repository you grant access to, including repositories that only use Dependabot security updates and don’t have a dependabot.yml file.

To add a registry, go to your organization’s Settings, select Secrets and variables, then Private registries, and choose New private registry. If you used a placeholder token as a workaround, delete that registry and add it again with Anonymous authentication. This is necessary because you can’t change the authentication method of an existing registry.

The Anonymous option is now generally available on github.com and will be available in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about giving security features access to private registries and resolving a blocked host in a Dependabot update job.

title.rendered: Push attribution for commits in limited public preview

content.rendered:
GitHub now durably records the authenticated user who pushed each commit and surfaces that pusher identity in the UI and API alongside the existing author and committer fields.

Commit author and committer fields are just strings that the pushing client supplies, so anyone with write access to a repository can set them to any name and email they choose. That makes it possible for an attacker who compromises a low-privilege account to forge commits that appear to come from a trusted maintainer, evading review policies and confusing audit trails. GitHub already authenticates pushes. This release adds durable, per-commit pusher attribution alongside the author and committer metadata.

With this release:

  • Every commit pushed to a repository now has a durable, authenticated pusher identity attached to it, independent of whatever the author and committer metadata claims.
  • A new repository rule condition, Committer must match pusher, blocks pushes where the committer metadata doesn’t match any verified email address of the authenticated pusher. This closes a path for commit identity spoofing.

You can use the pusher identity to spot-check suspicious activity or speed up security investigations instead of relying on unverified metadata. You can do this because the pusher identity is now visible wherever commits are shown instead. To enforce stricter identity requirements on a repository, add the new Committer must match pusher rule to a ruleset.

Push attribution is available now as a limited public preview for GitHub Enterprise customers. If you are interested in joining the preview, please contact your account team and request access.

Learn more about configuring push rulesets.

title.rendered: Improved detection for withdrawn Dependabot alerts

content.rendered:
You can now more easily detect withdrawn Dependabot alerts. Dependabot withdraws and removes an alert when the advisory or vulnerability that produced it is no longer valid. Two changes help you detect these withdrawals:

  • Webhooks: The dependabot_alert webhook event now includes a withdrawn action. The payload contains identifiers captured before the alert was removed, such as the alert number, GHSA and CVE IDs, package, and manifest path. If you already subscribe to dependabot_alert events, you’ll automatically receive these deliveries.
  • REST API: Requests to get or update a withdrawn alert now return 410 Gone instead of 404 Not Found, so you can tell a withdrawn alert apart from one that never existed.

These changes are available for all repositories on github.com and will be included in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.24.

Learn more about the dependabot_alert webhook event and the REST API endpoints for Dependabot alerts.

title.rendered: Repository security advisory comments API in public preview

content.rendered:
You can now read, add, and edit comments on repository security advisories using the REST API, including advisories created from private vulnerability reports.

Until now, the discussion on an advisory was only reachable in the web UI, even though it often holds the most useful triage context on a vulnerability report. With the new endpoints, you can:

  • List the comments on a repository security advisory, optionally limited to those updated since a given time.
  • Get a single comment.
  • Add a comment.
  • Edit a comment.

Repository security advisory responses also now include a comments count, and global advisory responses include the count for their linked repository advisory, so you can tell which advisories have discussion before you fetch it. These fields count non-confidential comments and help identify advisories with comment activity before fetching the comments.

This helps you export advisory discussions for audits and migrations, automatically add triage notes, and build advisory workflows that work the same way as the ones you already have for issues and pull requests.

A few things to know:

  • Access follows the same rules as the advisory itself. You need the repository security advisories scope, and anyone who can’t see an advisory can’t see its comments.
  • Access requires permission to view the advisory and the appropriate read or write repository security advisories permission or token scope. Non-collaborators cannot view internal comments, and confidential comments are not returned by these REST endpoints.
  • Deleting comments isn’t supported yet through the API.

This is available in public preview for public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

Learn more in our REST API docs.

title.rendered: New fields for SecurityAdvisory GraphQL API

content.rendered:
You can now read more of the GitHub Advisory Database directly from the GraphQL API without falling back to the REST API.

The SecurityAdvisory object gained five new fields:

  • cveId: The advisory’s CVE identifier.
  • sourceCodeLocation: A link to the affected source code relevant to the advisory.
  • githubReviewedAt: When GitHub reviewed the advisory.
  • nvdPublishedAt: When the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) published its record.
  • repositoryAdvisoryUrl: A link to the linked repository security advisory when there is one.

The securityAdvisories query also gained two new filters, severities and isWithdrawn, so you can narrow results on the server instead of downloading everything and filtering it yourself. They work alongside the filters you already use, such as classification, identifier, EPSS, and published or updated since.

This means fewer round trips, one authentication path, and one rate limit budget for integrations that read advisory data. It also makes it easier to build things like severity-based triage feeds, withdrawn advisory audits, and tracking of how quickly advisories move from NVD publication to GitHub review.

These changes are additive and read-only, so your existing queries keep working.

Learn more in the GraphQL API documentation and share your feedback.

title.rendered: Stateless GitHub App installation tokens rolled out

content.rendered:
The staged rollout of the stateless GitHub App installation token format, which began on April 27, 2026, is complete. By default, all newly minted GitHub App installation tokens will be in the stateless ghs_APPID_JWT format, which makes token issuance and validation faster and improves the reliability of the GitHub API.

What’s changed

Installation tokens still start with the ghs_ prefix, but they’re now about 520 characters long instead of 40.

Token permissions, repository scoping, the one-hour expiration, and the installation access token REST API endpoint are unchanged. Tokens minted before the change continue to work until they expire.

What to expect going forward

The temporary X-GitHub-Stateless-S2S-Token request header, which we introduced so you could validate the new format on demand, will be deprecated on November 30, 2026. After that date, GitHub will no longer respect the header, and all eligible apps will always receive stateless tokens. To learn more about the temporary header, see our original changelog for its release.

Once you’ve validated your apps and workflows with both token formats, remove the header from your production code before November 30, 2026.

Check your integrations

If you haven’t already, confirm that every system that handles installation tokens treats them as opaque strings. Look for:

  • Validation that requires tokens to be exactly 40 characters or patterns written for the legacy format.
  • Database columns, secret stores, or environment variables with a fixed or small maximum length.
  • Proxies, gateways, or middleware that truncate or reject long Authorization headers.
  • Logging and secret redaction rules that only match the legacy token pattern.

To learn more, see Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App.

title.rendered: Local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot now generally available

content.rendered:
Local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot is now generally available in GitHub Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and VS Code sessions using Agent Host.

Local sandboxes give developers a secure execution boundary for agentic workflows on their own machines. Tools and commands initiated by Copilot run with restricted access to the filesystem, network, credentials, and other system capabilities, based on policies defined by the developer or their organization.

Local sandboxing is powered by Microsoft eXecution Container (MXC), which translates a common sandbox policy into native operating-system controls across Windows, macOS, and Linux.

With local sandboxing, developers and organizations can:

  • Limit the files and directories that agent-run commands can read or modify.
  • Control access to the internet, local networks, Git credentials, and GitHub CLI credentials.
  • Apply sandboxing to local tools and services, including local MCP and language servers where supported.
  • Use enterprise-managed settings to require sandboxing and enforce policies that developers cannot weaken.
  • Adopt more autonomous agent workflows while maintaining clear boundaries around what Copilot can access.

Model execution and tool isolation are separate concerns. Sandbox policies apply to tool execution regardless of which model Copilot uses.

Local sandboxing is included with GitHub Copilot at no additional cost. To get started, see About cloud and local sandboxes for GitHub Copilot.

title.rendered: Structured forms for private vulnerability reports

content.rendered:
Private vulnerability reports can now use a structured form that asks reporters for the details you need to assess a vulnerability, including a reproducible proof of concept.

A single free-text box made it easy to submit low-quality or AI-generated reports and hard for you to find the signal in them. Now, by default, reporters must fill in four required fields: summary, details, proof of concept (at least 150 characters), and impact. Their answers are combined into the advisory description, so you review and edit the report as you do today.

With this update:

  • You can customize the form by adding a .github/VULNERABILITY_REPORT.yml file to your repository’s default branch. To apply a form to all repositories you own, add it to your organization or account’s .github repository. Forms use issue form syntax, and fields support min_length so you can require a minimum level of detail. If your form is invalid, the default form is used.
  • You can require reporters to assign a CWE before they submit, from Settings > Advanced Security > Private vulnerability reporting. Organization and enterprise owners can enforce this setting through a policy.
  • If your repository has a security policy, reporters see a banner linking to your SECURITY.md before they submit.
  • Reporters can check “I used AI assistance to find or write up this report” to disclose AI use.

If you add a custom form, reports submitted through the REST API must match it. The default form isn’t enforced for the API, so existing integrations keep working. When an API submission doesn’t match, the error points to a new endpoint that returns the form your repository enforces.

This is available for public repositories with private vulnerability reporting enabled on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

Learn more about privately reporting a security vulnerability.

title.rendered: npm staged publishing now supports creating new packages

content.rendered:
You can now create a new npm package with npm stage publish, using a local session or a granular access token, including a stage-only token. This lets you create packages from your automated workflows without a manual first publish.

This works for public scoped and unscoped packages, and private scoped packages. Your first version enters the staged queue and requires a maintainer to promote it before that version becomes available to install. After package creation, you can manage its settings and configure trusted publishing.

Learn more about staged publishing.

Join the npm roadmap discussion in GitHub Community to share feedback and discuss what’s next.

title.rendered: Unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations now expire

content.rendered:
Unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations now expire 48 hours after creation and can no longer authorize publishing. This limits the risk of trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership.

Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish. Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window—ordinary edits don’t restart the deadline.

If your configuration expires, recreate it to start a new 48-hour window. Expired configurations remain visible in trusted publisher settings but don’t count toward per-package limits. Other valid configurations on the package are unaffected.

npm also now rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events, alongside the existing pull_request_target restriction. If affected, move publishing to a permitted event such as push, release, or workflow_dispatch.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

title.rendered: GitHub Actions: macOS 14 runner image retirement

content.rendered:
The macOS 14 runner image will be retired on November 2, 2026. To raise awareness of the upcoming removal, jobs using macOS 14 will temporarily fail during the following scheduled brownout periods:

  • October 5, 14:00 UTC to October 6, 00:00 UTC
  • October 12, 14:00 UTC to October 13, 00:00 UTC
  • October 16, 14:00 UTC to October 17, 00:00 UTC
  • October 19, 14:00 UTC to October 20, 00:00 UTC
  • October 23, 14:00 UTC to October 24, 00:00 UTC
  • October 26, 14:00 UTC to October 27, 00:00 UTC
  • October 29, 14:00 UTC to October 30, 00:00 UTC
  • October 30, 14:00 UTC to October 31, 00:00 UTC

This deprecation includes the following labels:

  • macos-14
  • macos-14-large
  • macos-14-xlarge

During the lead-up to retirement, GitHub may reduce macOS 14 runner capacity, which could result in longer queue times for jobs that continue to use these labels.

What you need to do

Update your workflow files to use one of the following macOS arm64 labels:

  • macos-latest (macos-26)
  • macos-15
  • macos-latest-xlarge (macos-26-xlarge)
  • macos-15-xlarge

For up-to-date information about available tools and software, see the runner images repository. If you run into problems or need help, contact GitHub Support.

title.rendered: Rate limits for private vulnerability reports

content.rendered:
Open source maintainers are receiving more low-quality and automated vulnerability reports, which can bury the reports that matter. Rate limits cap how many new reports a single account can submit in a day, both to your repository and across GitHub. This helps protect you from bulk and automated submissions, while legitimate researchers can still reach you.

With this update:

  • Private vulnerability reporting now applies daily per-user rate limits to new reports.
  • Reporters who reach a limit see a message asking them to try again later.
  • Limits apply only to new reports. Comments on existing advisories aren’t affected.
  • Repository administrators can set a custom daily overall reporting limit for their repository.
  • Repository administrators can add trusted reporters to an allow list so they’re never rate limited.

To configure these settings, go to your repository’s settings, select Advanced Security, and click Settings next to “Private vulnerability reporting.”

This is available for public repositories with private vulnerability reporting enabled on GitHub Free, GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

Learn more in our docs about configuring private vulnerability reporting.

title.rendered: Actions retention now covers checks, runs, and statuses

content.rendered:
As previously announced, checks, workflow runs, and statuses are now governed by the same GitHub Actions retention setting that controls how long artifacts and logs are kept.

These records are automatically cleaned up when they exceed the retention period configured for your enterprise, organization, or repository. This applies to checks and statuses created by GitHub Actions and third-party applications.

The setting is labeled “Check, workflow run, status, artifact and log retention” in the UI. Repository retention remains subject to organization and enterprise caps, and the maximum retention for public repositories is 90 days. Changing the setting won’t restore data that was previously removed.

Review or update the artifact and log retention period for your repository. The expanded retention policy applies to GitHub Actions on github.com.

title.rendered: Actions Runner Controller release 0.15.0

content.rendered:
GitHub Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 includes reliability, scalability, and observability improvements for runner scale sets.

These updates help you operate larger runner fleets with fewer disruptions during upgrades and Kubernetes API updates. Here’s what’s now available:

  • Patch version upgrades now update resources in place, reducing disruption between autoscaling runner sets and ephemeral runner sets.
  • Controller shutdown behavior is more reliable because terminationGracePeriodSeconds is configurable and now aligns with the controller manager graceful shutdown timeout.
  • Runner scale sets can be reregistered when the recorded scale set no longer exists in the Actions service.
  • Controller updates now use patch requests instead of full update requests, reducing Kubernetes API payload size.
  • Runner status aggregation has moved to metrics for EphemeralRunnerSet and AutoscalingRunnerSet, reducing status patch requests.
  • Listener Kubernetes client rate limits are configurable through QPS and burst settings.
  • Controller concurrency can now be configured globally and per controller with max-concurrent-reconciles flags.
  • Controllers now filter incoming events so they perform fewer reconciliations than before.
  • Ephemeral runners are deleted faster because the server-side check for runner removal is skipped when the runner pod successfully exits.

These changes are especially useful for clusters with many runner scale sets where controller throughput, graceful shutdown, and accurate metrics are important for day-to-day operations.

Learn more in the Actions Runner Controller documentation.

title.rendered: Opt-in dist-tag permissions for npm trusted publishing

content.rendered:
Trusted publishing configurations for npm can now be granted permission to manage dist-tags (e.g., promoting a version to latest, updating next and beta pointers) using short-lived OIDC credentials instead of a long-lived access token.

Previously, trusted publishing covered publishing and staging, but not dist-tag operations. That meant maintainers who had otherwise fully moved to token-free, OIDC-based workflows still had to keep a granular access token around solely to manage tags after a release or a rollback.

  • Each trusted publishing configuration now has an opt-in Allow npm dist-tag permission. It defaults to off for both new and existing configurations, so no configuration automatically gains new capability.
  • The permission is independent of direct publishing, so a staging-only configuration can also be granted dist-tag management.
  • A dist-tag operation is authorized if the incoming OIDC token matches any one configuration with the permission enabled.
  • Existing token-based dist-tag management continues to work unchanged.

To use it, open your package’s trusted publishing settings and enable Allow npm dist-tag on the configurations that should be able to manage tags.

Learn more about trusted publishers for npm.

Join the discussion within our roadmap discussions.

title.rendered: Repository custom runner settings for Dependabot

content.rendered:
As a repository administrator, you can now configure the runner type, optional custom label, and optional runner group for Dependabot version and security updates. This extends the runner configuration already available at the organization level, giving you more control over where each repository’s Dependabot jobs run.

Labeled runners can target both self-hosted and larger GitHub-hosted runners suited to your project’s needs, such as access to private package registries or specialized environments.

These repository-level settings are available for private and internal repositories on github.com. The controls are hidden for public repositories and on GitHub Enterprise Server.

To get started, open your repository settings and select Advanced Security. Under “Dependency scanning”, find “Dependabot version updates”, then edit Runner type. Choose Labeled runner, then optionally enter a custom label and runner group. If you do not specify a label, Dependabot uses the dependabot label. Alternatively, choose Standard GitHub runner to use the default GitHub-hosted environment.

Security configurations do not currently enforce Dependabot runner settings.

Check out the docs to learn more about using custom labels with self-hosted runners and managing Dependabot on self-hosted runners.

title.rendered: Bring business context with external custom properties

content.rendered:
You can now seamlessly bring business context about your repositories from an external system of record (e.g., a configuration management database (CMDB), an internal developer portal, or an in-house system) into GitHub with external custom properties. This feature is now in public preview.

Keep business context aligned with its source, with updates managed by your external system. This includes information such as ownership, service tier, lifecycle stage, and compliance status.

When to choose external custom properties

Use custom properties when you want to manage this context in GitHub, whether through the UI or APIs. Choose external custom properties when an external system should exclusively own and continuously update that context:

  • Read-only in the GitHub UI: Users can’t edit these values in GitHub, preventing conflicting updates across systems.
  • Ongoing synchronization: Your external integration uses the external custom properties APIs to keep values current as your source data changes.
  • Dedicated namespace: Your integration manages properties under its own prefix, keeping them separate from properties managed by other sources.

You can use external custom properties everywhere you use custom properties today, including repository views, repository filtering, and ruleset targeting. Your existing governance can use the synced business context while your external system remains the source of truth.

Connect your system of record

Port.io is the first partner to integrate with external custom properties. Read Port.io’s announcement for an overview, or follow the Port.io integration guide to sync your business context to GitHub.

You aren’t limited to partner integrations. Any enterprise can build its own integration using the external custom properties APIs, with fine-grained permissions to control its access. To get started, see Integrating custom properties with an external system.

Join the conversation in the GitHub Community announcements category.

title.rendered: Self-hosted runner version enforcement date has moved

content.rendered:
The enforcement date for GitHub Actions minimum version requirements for self-hosted runners on GitHub Enterprise Cloud has changed. The change ships Monday, September 28, 2026, and full enforcement now begins Tuesday, September 29, 2026. This is instead of the date that was previously announced.

The requirements themselves are unchanged:

  • Self-hosted runners below version 2.329.0 won’t be able to register or reregister.
  • Existing runners below the minimum version required to execute workflow jobs (which is a higher version than the registration minimum) will stop running jobs, even if they were previously registered.

If you haven’t upgraded your self-hosted runners yet, do so before September 29, 2026 to avoid disruption to your workflows. See the self-hosted runner documentation for upgrade guidance. You can also use the new REST API for runner version deprecations to check the registration and runtime deprecation dates for any runner version and build automated alerts for fleets nearing their deadline.

This shift only affects GitHub Enterprise Cloud. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t impacted. Enforcement already began for GitHub Enterprise Cloud with Data Residency on July 31, 2026.

title.rendered: Changes to query results in the GitHub Actions API and UI

content.rendered:
Queries for workflow runs in the GitHub Actions API and UI now return a less precise but more accurate count of records when you search by workflow, event, status, branch, or actor. We will continue to return paginated results of up to 1,000 items. However, if the number of found records exceeds 2,500, we will report “2,500+” instead of attempting to return the exact number of records. This is because queries that retrieve more than 2,500 records frequently timeout and return the number of records found before the timeout rather than the true count. By implementing this limit, our counts will be more accurate and we will improve performance for customers.

If your integrations or scripts rely on retrieving more than 2,500 matching workflow runs from a single query, narrow your filters (e.g., by adding a date range) to retrieve the specific runs you need. This change is rolling out now on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

title.rendered: Expired GitHub Actions artifacts no longer shown in UI and API

content.rendered:
Expired artifacts are no longer displayed in the GitHub Actions run summary or returned by the REST API. Previously, an expired artifact remained visible with an “Expired” pill, even though the underlying files had already been deleted from storage.

That leftover pill left some users unsure whether they were still being billed for storing artifacts that no longer existed. To remove that ambiguity, expired artifacts will not be shown when viewing run data, including:

  • The list of artifacts on a workflow run summary page.
  • The list artifacts for a repository and get an artifact REST API endpoints.

If you need to know which artifacts a workflow run produced after they’ve expired, you can still find that information in the run’s logs. This change doesn’t affect artifact retention settings or billing—it only changes how expired artifacts are displayed.

title.rendered: Node 20 is no longer available in GitHub Actions

content.rendered:
This is the final notification that Node 20 is no longer available on GitHub Actions runners. Runners now use Node 24 for JavaScript actions. The temporary ACTIONS_ALLOW_USE_UNSECURE_NODE_VERSION opt-out is no longer available.

If you maintain a JavaScript action, update its runs.using value to node24 and publish a new release as soon as possible. For details, see the metadata syntax for JavaScript actions.

If you use JavaScript actions in your workflows, update to the latest versions of those actions that support Node 24. For details, see using versions for actions.

The newest versions of all first-party actions were updated to use Node 24 as referenced in our announcement changelog.

Node 24 is incompatible with macOS 13.4 and earlier, and it doesn’t officially support ARM32. Self-hosted runners using these operating systems or architectures are no longer supported. This change applies to github.com and GitHub with Data Residency.

title.rendered: npm extends recovery-code security holds to all accounts

content.rendered:
npm now places a temporary 72-hour security hold on any account after a successful recovery-code sign-in, extending a protection that previously applied only to high-impact accounts. This change applies to all npm accounts.

During the hold, publishing and other security-sensitive writes, including creating access tokens, are paused. You can still sign in as well as browse and install packages. The hold expires automatically — no action or support request is needed to restore full access.

This extension builds on the preventive account protection npm introduced for high-impact accounts, further slowing account-takeover attempts and reducing the risk of malicious publishing from a compromised recovery code.

If you’re unexpectedly blocked from publishing and you didn’t use your recovery code to sign in, contact npm Support right away.

title.rendered: Stage-only npm tokens for safer automation

content.rendered:
You can now select Read and write (stage only) when creating an npm granular access token. This lets your automated workflows stage package versions for review without giving the token permission to publish new versions directly to the npm registry.

Your workflow uses npm stage publish to submit a version. A package maintainer then reviews and approves its release with two-factor authentication (2FA). npm rejects direct npm publish attempts with that token, even if you’ve configured it to bypass 2FA for automation.

Stage-only tokens retain other package write permissions, including moving dist-tags and deprecating versions. Protect them with the same care as any other write token.

Prepare your automation for the token transition

This release is opt-in and doesn’t change existing tokens or their direct-publish capabilities.

As previously announced, npm is targeting January 2027 to remove direct publishing through bypass-2FA tokens. If you can’t move to trusted publishing yet, stage-only tokens offer a migration path for token-based automation.

To get started:

  1. Create a granular access token with Read and write (stage only) permissions for the packages your workflow needs.
  2. Replace your workflow’s publishing token and use npm stage publish instead of npm publish.
  3. Have a maintainer review and approve staged versions with 2FA.

Staged publishing works with existing npm packages. You’ll need publish access to the package, 2FA enabled on your npm account, npm CLI 11.15.0 or later, and Node.js 22.14.0 or later.

Learn more about staged publishing, and share questions or migration blockers in the npm community discussion category.

title.rendered: Ubuntu 26 generally available and latest migration

content.rendered:
The Ubuntu 26.04 runner image for GitHub Actions is now out of public preview and fully supported for production workflows on both x64 and arm64. As part of this release, the ubuntu-latest label will migrate to Ubuntu 26.04, giving you the latest supported Ubuntu release by default.

Using Ubuntu 26.04

To run your workflows on the new image, set runs-on: ubuntu-26.04 or runs-on: ubuntu-26.04-arm in your workflow file. Ubuntu 26.04 includes updated, and in some cases removed, tools and tool versions compared to earlier images. These changes can break workflows that depend on specific software versions or preinstalled packages. Review the full list of changes and test your workflows against Ubuntu 26 before the migration begins.

ubuntu-latest is migrating to Ubuntu 26.04

The ubuntu-latest label will migrate from Ubuntu 24.04 to Ubuntu 26.04. This migration will roll out gradually between October 19 and November 19, 2026. During this window, workflows that use ubuntu-latest will automatically move to Ubuntu 26.04.

Because this moves your workflows to a new operating system version, the migration may break builds that rely on tools, packages, or versions that changed between Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. To prepare:

  • Test your workflows against ubuntu-26.04 before the migration begins.
  • If you are not ready to move, pin your workflows to ubuntu-24.04 to stay on the current image.

Learn more

To learn more about available images, see the GitHub-hosted runners documentation. To see the included software list or report issues with the image, head to the runner-images repository.

title.rendered: Actions retention will cover checks, workflow runs, and statuses

content.rendered:
Starting October 1, 2026, checks, workflow runs, and statuses will be governed by the same Actions retention setting that already controls how long artifacts and logs are kept, with a default of 90 days. Until now, checks, workflow runs, and statuses were retained for 400+ days regardless of your retention configuration. After this change, they will automatically be cleaned up once they pass the artifact and log retention period configured for your repository, organization, or enterprise.

This change reduces the amount of stale data stored across GitHub Actions, helping keep checks, workflow runs, and statuses fast and reliable for everyone.

What’s changing

  • Checks, workflow runs, and statuses will follow your Actions retention setting. They will be cleaned up once they exceed your configured artifact and log retention period, instead of sticking around for 400+ days. This applies to checks and statuses created by Actions as well as third-party applications.
  • The retention setting now has a broader scope. The setting label in the UI will be updated to read “Check, workflow run, status, artifact and log retention” to reflect that it now governs all five.
  • Retention caps still apply. A repository can raise its retention only up to the cap configured at the organization and enterprise level. For public repositories, the maximum retention for checks, workflow runs, and statuses is 90 days, matching the existing limit for artifacts and logs.
  • The change is not retroactive. Adjusting your retention setting will not restore data that was previously evicted due to a retention policy. This matches how artifact and log retention behaves today.

Editor’s note (September 15th, 2026): Added clarification about which checks and statuses are impacted.

Billing and storage implications

Artifacts and logs count toward your billable GitHub Actions storage. Because this change cleans up data once it passes your retention period, repositories that previously kept artifacts and logs around longer than their configured setting may see a reduction in billable Actions storage usage.

Keep this in mind when you review your retention setting:

  • Lowering your retention period removes artifacts and logs sooner, which can reduce your Actions storage costs.
  • Raising your retention period keeps artifacts and logs available longer, which may increase your billable Actions storage. Checks, workflow run, and statuses metadata are not billed for storage, but the artifacts and logs associated with them are.

What you need to do

For most repositories, no action is required. Starting on October 1, checks, workflow runs, and statuses will be cleaned up according to the retention setting you already have configured.

To prepare:

  • Review your Actions retention setting for your repository, organization, or enterprise before October 1, 2026. Confirm it reflects how long you need checks, workflow runs, and statuses to remain available.
  • Increase the retention period if you need a longer window, up to the maximum allowed by your organization and enterprise caps (90 days for public repositories). Note that a longer retention period keeps artifacts and logs longer and may increase your billable Actions storage.
  • Export or archive anything you need to keep beyond your configured retention period, since older checks, workflow runs, and statuses will be automatically removed once this change takes effect.

title.rendered: Block pull requests with exposed secrets from merging

content.rendered:
Repository rulesets allow you to easily add scalable protections across your repositories. Starting today, you can use repository rulesets to block pull requests from merging when the pull request introduces secret scanning alerts.

What’s new

You can enable the new rule require secret scanning alerts are resolved on pull requests for selected repositories. Developers without bypass permissions must clear the block by resolving each alert.

The rule checks two things before a pull request can merge:

  • A secret scan has completed for the head commit
  • No alerts are open for secrets introduced by the pull request’s commits

By default, the rule runs on open pull requests and blocks secrets found via provider patterns. You can additionally configure the rule to block other categories (e.g., custom or generic patterns).

This rule is available today in public preview for customers with GitHub Secret Protection or GitHub Advanced Security.

How this rule differs from push protection

Push protection stops a secret at the push, before it ever reaches the repository. This rule adds an additional layer of protection at the pull request layer, catching cases that push protection isn’t able to or configured to catch. For example, you may keep push protection disabled for generic pattern secret types, while keeping a ruleset to block pull requests for those secret types.

How to configure the rule

  1. In your repository, organization, or enterprise settings, go to the Repository > Rulesets tab.
  2. Create or edit a ruleset targeting the branches you want to protect.
  3. Select Require secret scanning alerts are resolved.

You can also configure the rule through the REST API using the require_secret_scanning_alert_resolution rule type with a secret_types parameter, or through GraphQL as REQUIRE_SECRET_SCANNING_ALERT_RESOLUTION.

Learn more

Learn more about secret scanning and push protection in our documentation.

See the rulesets documentation for how rules are applied and bypassed.

title.rendered: Control GitHub Actions cache access with cache-mode

content.rendered:
You can now use cache-mode to apply least-privilege access to the GitHub Actions cache at the workflow or job level. By granting each workflow or job only the cache access it needs, you can prevent unnecessary restores or saves and help protect trusted workflows from cache poisoning. This capability is now generally available on all plans.

Choose the access each workflow or job needs:

  • read allows cache restores but prevents cache saves. This is the default for low-trust events such as pull_request_target.
  • write allows cache restores and saves. This is the default for trusted events such as push.
  • write-only allows cache saves but prevents cache restores.
  • none prevents all cache access.

Job-level settings override workflow-level settings. The selected mode is enforced by the cache service and carries through reusable workflows, where a called workflow cannot receive more cache access than its caller granted.

An explicitly declared cache-mode also overrides the read-only cache default for low-trust events such as pull_request_target. Declaring write or write-only for these events can increase the risk of cache poisoning, so GitHub Actions adds a warning annotation when the declared mode grants write access. Workflows that do not set cache-mode continue to use the existing secure defaults.

Cache mode is generally available on github.com for all GitHub plans. For configuration details, see the cache-mode workflow syntax documentation.
